summary: The incident is best modeled as MySQL CPU saturation from a read-heavy benchmark dominated by inefficient multi-table joins, high concurrency, and missing supporting indexes on join/filter columns; query-cache churn may have been an additional factor in the original environment.
symptoms: MySQL consumed most CPU time while the web servers did not show comparable load.
The benchmark was read-heavy and the database became the bottleneck.
MySQLTuner reported many joins without indexes and very poor table-cache hit rate.
Query cache efficiency was low and pruning was extremely frequent in the posted environment.
OS sampling showed high user-space CPU usage on the database VM.
mechanism: Concurrent read-only queries drive CPU-heavy nested-loop style join work across a large fact table and smaller dimension tables, with selective predicates on unindexed columns and fanout from the item table. The original post also suggests query-cache mutex pressure and connection churn as possible amplifiers, but the core reproducible mechanism is join fanout plus missing indexes under concurrency.

facts.evidence: The post states the server is running MySQL 5.5.47 on Ubuntu 12.04.
The post says the VM has 5 vCPU and 4 GB of memory.
The poster says they are benchmarking web-server queries and the Tuner output shows 100% reads / 0% writes.
vmstat shows high user CPU and the poster reports the database is the bottleneck.
The post includes the query cache settings and MySQLTuner reports low efficiency with very frequent pruning.
MySQLTuner reports highest connection usage at 100% with 152 of 151 max threads reached.
The accepted and top-voted answers point to unindexed joins, inefficient queries, and possible mutex/locking contention.
The strongest common mechanism across the post is read-heavy multi-table joins with insufficient indexes and high concurrent load.

assumptions: The exact production schema is unknown, so a synthetic star-schema workload is used to preserve join fanout and filter selectivity.
The main reproducible issue is CPU burn from join work rather than a storage-engine-specific bug.
Query-cache contention may have existed in production, but the current target environment does not need it to reproduce the primary symptom.
The benchmark can be approximated with a single dominant read query class repeated at concurrency.
unknowns: The exact application SQL and its parameter distributions are unknown.
The original index layout is unknown beyond the strong hint that many joins lacked indexes.
Whether the posted environment had query cache contention versus pure query inefficiency is not known.
Whether the database used mostly InnoDB or mixed engines in the benchmark is not fully specified.
